title: Flatbread Proof funding for a part-time maintainer
framing:
You are one node in a second Oven DAG run for the Flatbread project. The first run produced `internal/funding/README.md`, a report on 118 funding and support programs. It scored them without knowing who would apply. Now we know. This run re-screens that report against the real applicant and researches the routes the first run could not see.

TODAY IS 23 AUGUST 2026. Your training data stops before that. Treat every date, amount, program status and eligibility rule you remember as a lead to check, never as a fact to report. Every claim you write must come from a page you opened during this run, or from a file in this repository. When you cannot open a page, mark the claim `UNVERIFIED` and say why.

## The applicant, stated by the maintainer

- One individual: Tony Ketcham, working as FlatbreadLabs.
- He holds a full-time job and **will keep it**. Proof is side work. This is settled, not a phase.
- He is open to co-maintainers and to other individual contributors joining.
- He is evangelising Proof inside his employer, so contributions from colleagues at that employer are plausible.
- Employer identity is UNKNOWN. Do not guess it, name it, or infer it. Whether that employer runs an open-source fund, an employee award programme, a contribution policy, or claims intellectual property in side projects is UNKNOWN and is a question for Tony.
- Legal entity and country of residence remain UNKNOWN, as in the first run.

## What this profile rules out

Screen these out, whatever their award size. Say which rule fired and quote the requirement with its URL.

1. **Full-time commitment.** Any programme that requires the applicant to work on the project full-time, leave employment, or certify full-time availability.
2. **Relocation, residency or on-site attendance.** Any cohort, residency, fellowship or accelerator that requires living in or travelling to a named place for weeks or months.
3. **Venture-scale founding.** Any programme that presumes the applicant will found a venture-backed company, take an equity investment on those terms, or pursue a startup path full-time. Proof is a public-good library, and Tony is not leaving his job to run a company.

A programme that merely *permits* part-time work, or that only asks for a few hours a week, is not screened out. Read the published rule before you cut it. Where a programme is silent on time commitment, say `UNKNOWN` and treat it as a question, not a disqualification.

## What this profile adds

Two things the first run never considered. Research both properly.

1. **The employer as a constraint.** An employment contract may assign intellectual property in side projects to the employer, and may restrict outside income. Many funders ask the applicant to warrant that they own or can license the work, or to declare conflicting obligations. Flag every programme whose terms touch IP ownership, exclusivity, or outside employment, and say exactly what it asks.
2. **The employer as a route.** Colleagues contributing means contributors from a second organisation, which several foundations require. Some companies run open-source funds, dependency-sponsorship programmes, or employee-nominated awards that only an employee can start. Research those routes concretely.

## What the project needs, re-ordered for this profile

Money is no longer needed to replace a salary. It is needed for evaluation spend, for collaborator or contractor time, and for project costs. So:

1. **Comped AI spend** rises to first. Model credits and compute to run recall evaluations across several model families. This is the live blocker and it costs Tony no time to receive.
2. **Exposure that brings contributors**, not just users. A co-maintainer is worth more than a star.
3. **Cash**, weighted by how little of Tony's time it consumes. A £50,000 grant with a month of reporting is worth less to a part-time maintainer than £5,000 with none.

Mid to long term the project wants funded room to research the knowledge-graph side of agent memory: what structure an agent's memory should have, how to keep recall bounded as the graph grows, and how to measure whether stored reasoning changes a later agent's behaviour.

## Program entry schema

Write every programme as one `###` heading naming it, then exactly these labelled lines in this order. Write `UNKNOWN` when a page does not say. Never guess.

- `Funder` — the organisation behind the money or credits.
- `Track` — the exact named programme or call.
- `Support type` — one or more of `CASH`, `AI-CREDITS`, `CLOUD-CREDITS`, `EXPOSURE`, `CONTRIBUTORS`, `MENTORSHIP`, `EQUITY-INVESTMENT`.
- `Award` — amount or range with currency, and what it may be spent on.
- `Time commitment` — what the programme demands of the applicant after acceptance, in hours or days. This is the field that decides most of this run, so never leave it `UNKNOWN` without saying you looked.
- `Time cost to apply` — working days of Tony's own time the application needs.
- `IP and employment terms` — what it asks about ownership, licensing, exclusivity or outside work, or `none found`.
- `Applicant type required` — individual, unincorporated project, company, non-profit, fiscal host, academic, or a named country.
- `Status` — `OPEN`, `ROLLING`, `CLOSED` or `NEXT-CALL-UNANNOUNCED`, as of 23 August 2026.
- `Deadline` — next deadline with its year, or the cadence for a rolling call. Write `PASSED: <date>` when the last call closed.
- `How to apply` — numbered steps and the exact form or contact URL.
- `Opportunity` — an integer 0 to 100 from the rubric below, with the four sub-scores. When the programme appears in `internal/funding/README.md`, add `(was <n> in the first report)` and one clause saying why it moved.
- `Confidence` — an integer 0 to 100 from the rubric below, with the reason.
- `Fit verdict` — `STRONG`, `PLAUSIBLE`, `WEAK` or `INELIGIBLE`, and the one sentence that decides it.
- `Pitch angle` — three to six sentences.
- `Evidence` — the URLs you opened, one per line.

## Opportunity rubric, 0 to 100, re-weighted for this profile

Add four sub-scores and show them as `credits/contributors/cash/research = a/b/c/d`.

- Comped AI or compute spend, 0 to 35: none 0; up to $5k 10; $5k to $25k 20; $25k to $100k 28; above $100k 35. Add nothing for credits the project cannot use, and say so when a programme's credits cover only one model family.
- Contributors and exposure that recruit, 0 to 25: judge by whether it brings maintainers, mentored contributors or a second contributing organisation — not by page views.
- Cash, net of the time it costs, 0 to 25: start from the award band (up to $5k 8; $5k to $25k 14; $25k to $100k 20; above $100k 25) then subtract for the reporting and application load a part-time maintainer must carry. Show the subtraction.
- Room for agent-memory and knowledge-graph research, 0 to 15: does the programme pay for research and evaluation, or only for shipping?

## Confidence rubric, 0 to 100

Confidence is the chance a strong application from **this applicant** is accepted. Bands: 80 to 100 `VERY HIGH`, 60 to 79 `HIGH`, 40 to 59 `MODERATE`, 20 to 39 `LOW`, 0 to 19 `VERY LOW`. Anchor each score on a published acceptance rate, a cohort size against an applicant count, or the programme's own stated bar. A programme this applicant cannot apply to scores 0. Where a programme values full-time dedication but does not require it, lower confidence and say so.

## Hard rules

- Never invent a programme, an amount, a deadline, or a URL. A missing fact is `UNKNOWN`.
- Never name or guess the employer. Write "Tony's employer".
- Do not give legal advice. On employment and IP questions, say what the funder asks and what Tony must check with his own employment agreement or a lawyer.
- Write only the one file your task names. Do not create or edit any other file.
- Do not run `git`. Do not stage, commit, branch, push, or install packages.
- Do not start servers. Do not run `pnpm build`, `pnpm test`, or the Flatbread CLI.
- Prefer the funder's own pages over a blog roundup. Say when your only source is second-hand.
- Write plain, concrete English: short words, short sentences, active voice. Do not write "leverage", "utilise", "revolutionise", "unlock the potential", or "game-changing".

tasks.subtask_prompt:
You re-screen the first report against the applicant profile. This is the single biggest change in this run, so be exhaustive and quote the rule you apply.

Read `internal/funding/README.md`. It holds 118 programmes under `## Program detail`, each with a `Strings attached`, `Applicant type required` and `Award` line. Also read its `## All programs by opportunity value` table for the full set. Search the web only to settle a time-commitment question a programme's page must answer.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/11-profile-rescreen.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Screened out by this profile`, `## Survives, with a caveat`, `## Survives cleanly`, `## Could not decide`, `## Coverage note`.

Method:

1. Walk every programme in `## Program detail`. For each, decide whether rule 1 (full-time commitment), rule 2 (relocation, residency or on-site attendance) or rule 3 (venture-scale founding) fires.
2. Do not cut a programme because it *prefers* dedication. Cut it only when the published rule requires full-time work, presence in a place, or founding a company. Where the report's own text is ambiguous, open the funder's page and settle it.
3. Note that the first report already scored many programmes confidence 0 for the entity gate. Those are still on the list — an entity can be formed, whereas Tony's employment is settled. Keep the two reasons apart: say `PROFILE` when this run's rules fire and `ENTITY` when only the old gate fires.

What each section holds:

- `## Screened out by this profile` — a Markdown table with columns `Program`, `Rule`, `The requirement`, `Source URL`. `Rule` is `FULL-TIME`, `RELOCATION` or `VENTURE-SCALE`. `The requirement` quotes or closely paraphrases the published rule. Use the programme's exact `###` heading text from `internal/funding/README.md` in the `Program` column so a later node can match it.
- `## Survives, with a caveat` — programmes a part-time maintainer can pursue but which cost real time or lower his odds. One bullet each: the programme, the caveat, and the hours or days it demands.
- `## Survives cleanly` — programmes with no time commitment beyond the application itself. One bullet each with the time cost to apply in working days.
- `## Could not decide` — programmes whose time commitment no page states. One bullet each with the question to ask the funder.
- `## Coverage note` — how many of the 118 you walked, how many each rule cut, how many survive, and where the report's own text was too thin to decide.

Count carefully and state the arithmetic: the four buckets must add to the number of programmes you walked.

You research the constraint the first run never considered: the applicant holds a full-time job, and that employment may reach into a side project.

Read `internal/funding/research/00-proof-fit-brief.md` for the project's facts. Then research the web.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/12-employer-ip.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## What funders ask`, `## Where Proof is exposed`, `## What Tony must check`, `## What the project should do`, `## Programs that need a second look`, `## Coverage note`.

Research these questions against real sources, and prefer funder and foundation pages over general legal blogs:

1. **What do funders actually ask about IP and outside employment?** Open the terms, FAQ or application guidance of the grant programmes an individual can apply to — NLnet, the Sovereign Tech Agency, GitHub's open-source funding, FUTO, FLOSS/fund, Open Collective and the Open Source Collective, Manifund, and the AI research funds — and record what each asks. Look for: a warranty that the applicant owns or may license the work; a declaration of conflicting obligations; rules on funding work an employer already pays for; rules on double funding; and requirements about who may receive the money.
2. **How do open-source foundations handle contributions from employees?** Find the published position of the Linux Foundation, the OpenJS Foundation, the Apache Software Foundation and the CNCF on contributor licence agreements, the Developer Certificate of Origin, and corporate contribution or employer sign-off. Give the exact documents.
3. **What do company open-source policies typically require of an employee contributing to an outside project?** Find real, published corporate open-source policy documents or contribution guides that state the approval path. Name the companies whose policies you actually opened.
4. **What is the accepted practice for a project that starts accepting contributions from a company?** Look at how comparable single-maintainer TypeScript or developer-tool projects handle a DCO or CLA, and what tooling exists (for example the DCO app, CLA assistant, or the Linux Foundation's EasyCLA).

What each section holds:

- `## What funders ask` — a Markdown table with `Funder or programme`, `What it asks about IP or outside work`, `Why it matters here`, `Source URL`. One row per programme you opened. Say `none found` in the second column where the terms are silent, and say which document you read to conclude that.
- `## Where Proof is exposed` — the concrete risks, worst first. Cover: an employment IP-assignment clause reaching a side project; a moonlighting or outside-income clause meeting grant money; a colleague committing from a work machine or on work time so the employer owns the copyright; and a funder's warranty Tony could not truthfully sign. For each, say what evidence would settle it.
- `## What Tony must check` — a numbered list of the exact documents and questions, in the order he should take them: his employment agreement, any IP assignment or invention-assignment schedule, his employer's open-source contribution policy, its outside-activity or moonlighting rules, and who inside the company can give written approval. Say plainly that this is not legal advice and that an employment lawyer should read the clauses before he signs a funder's IP warranty.
- `## What the project should do` — the repository changes that make outside and corporate contributions safe, in priority order, each with the tooling and the effort in hours. Cover the choice between a Developer Certificate of Origin and a contributor licence agreement, and say which suits a small MIT-licensed project and why. Note what `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `LICENSE` in this repository already say, and what is missing.
- `## Programs that need a second look` — programmes from `internal/funding/README.md` whose terms Tony cannot safely sign until the employment question is settled. Give the programme, the clause, and the URL.
- `## Coverage note` — how many pages you opened, which questions you could not answer from primary sources, and where your coverage is thin.

You research the routes that open up **because** the applicant has an employer and is evangelising Proof inside it. The first run never looked here.

Read `internal/funding/research/00-proof-fit-brief.md` for the project's facts. Then research the web.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/13-employer-routes.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Ranked programs`, `## How to start one from inside`, `## Screened out`, `## Coverage note`.

`## Ranked programs` holds one full entry per programme using the schema in the framing, sorted by opportunity, highest first.

Research these, and find more. Confirm current terms on the programme's own page; several of these change yearly or quietly close.

- **Employee-nominated award programmes**, where only someone inside a company can put a project forward. Find the current published programmes and their nomination rules. Start with the Google Open Source Peer Bonus and look for equivalents at other large employers.
- **Corporate open-source funds** that pay maintainers of dependencies the company uses. Find the published, currently-running ones and how a project gets considered. Start with the Microsoft FOSS Fund, the Indeed FOSS Fund, and the members of the Open Source Pledge, and check which publish a nomination or application route rather than picking privately.
- **Dependency-funding rails a company can switch on** for the projects it depends on: GitHub Sponsors for organisations, thanks.dev, Open Source Collective, Drips, Polar, and Tidelift. For each, say exactly what a company must do to start paying, and what the project must have in place first to receive it. This is the most actionable category, because Tony can advocate for it directly.
- **Programmes that require a contributing organisation**, which colleague contributions could satisfy. Note the published threshold and where it is recorded.
- **Conference and writing routes an employer sponsors**, where a company pays for a maintainer to speak about a project it uses.

`## How to start one from inside` is the practical section and the point of this task. Write a numbered path Tony can walk at his own employer without naming it: how to find whether the company already has an open-source programme office, a FOSS fund, a peer-bonus scheme or a dependency-sponsorship budget; who normally owns that budget; what a project must publish before a company will pay it; and what a short internal case for sponsoring Proof should contain. Ground every step in a real published corporate policy, programme page or foundation guide, and cite it. Where you are reasoning from general practice rather than a document, say so in that step.

`## Screened out` names routes you rejected with the reason and the URL. `## Coverage note` says how many pages you opened, how many entries you kept, and where coverage is thin.

You research comped AI spend for **an individual maintaining an open-source project with no company, no funding round and no academic affiliation**. This is the project's first need under the new profile and the live blocker on its evaluation work.

The first run found that most large credit programmes are startup or university programmes. Do not repeat that finding — go looking specifically for the open-source and individual-researcher routes it under-covered.

Read `internal/funding/research/00-proof-fit-brief.md` for the research agenda the credits must pay for. Read `internal/funding/README.md`'s `## Comped AI spend and compute` section so you do not simply restate it. Then research the web.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/14-oss-credits.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Ranked programs`, `## Model coverage table`, `## Screened out`, `## Leads not yet checked`, `## Coverage note`.

`## Ranked programs` holds one full entry per programme using the schema in the framing, sorted by opportunity, highest first. For every entry add two extra labelled lines after `Award`:

- `Credit value and expiry` — the dollar value, how long the credits last, and whether expiry leaves enough time for an evaluation a part-time maintainer runs on evenings and weekends.
- `Open-source route` — whether this is an open-source programme, a startup programme, an academic programme, or a general free tier. Say which, and quote the eligibility sentence.

Check every seed below, and find more. For each, be strict about one thing: does the published route admit an individual open-source maintainer with no company?

- Programmes named for open source rather than startups: OpenAI's Codex for open source, Anthropic's open-source offer, and any equivalent from Google, Microsoft, Meta or Mistral. Find the published dependency, download or contributor thresholds and state them exactly.
- Individual-researcher access: OpenAI's researcher access programme, Anthropic's external researcher access, Google's academic and research access, and any programme that admits an unaffiliated researcher.
- Open-weight inference hosts with an open-source or research route rather than a startup route: Together AI, Modal, Fireworks, Baseten, Groq, Cerebras, Replicate, Runpod, Nebius, Lambda, Arcee and OpenRouter. For each, find whether an OSS-specific route exists at all; if only a startup route exists, screen it out and say so.
- Free and community compute: Hugging Face ZeroGPU and community GPU grants, Google Colab and the TPU Research Cloud, Kaggle, and any public-good compute an individual may request.
- Agent-tool credits that would pay for the agent runs themselves rather than raw inference, including any open-source or maintainer offer from coding-agent vendors.
- Sustained free tiers generous enough to run a bounded evaluation. Say honestly when a free tier beats a credit programme for this use, because a free tier needs no application and costs no time.

`## Model coverage table` is the deliverable that decides the plan. The project's evaluation compares recall quality **across several model families**, so a programme covering one family is worth much less. Build a Markdown table with `Program`, `Families covered`, `Named models`, `Value`, `Expiry`, `Admits an individual OSS maintainer`, `Source URL`. Then write two or three sentences naming the smallest combination of programmes that would cover a cross-family evaluation, and roughly what it would cost if bought outright instead.

`## Screened out` names each programme you rejected with the reason and the URL. `## Leads not yet checked` names what you ran out of time on. `## Coverage note` says how many pages you opened, how many you kept, and where coverage is thin.

You research what changes now that co-maintainers and contributors from a second organisation are plausible. The first report screened several routes out for exactly this reason, so your job is to say precisely what threshold each one sets and what the shortest honest path to it is.

Read `internal/funding/research/00-proof-fit-brief.md` for the repository's governance and contributor gaps, and `internal/funding/README.md` for the programmes previously cut on community grounds. Then research the web.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/15-contributor-unlocks.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Thresholds table`, `## Ranked programs`, `## Shortest path`, `## Not worth it yet`, `## Coverage note`.

`## Thresholds table` is the core deliverable. A Markdown table with `Program`, `Published threshold`, `Where it is written`, `Proof today`, `Gap`, `Source URL`. Get the exact published numbers, not approximations, for at least these:

- Google Summer of Code, and its requirement for an established community of active contributors.
- The CNCF project lifecycle, and its maintainer count and organisational-diversity rules for Sandbox and Incubating.
- The OpenJS Foundation's new-project application, its at-large and incubation stages, and what governance and sponsorship it requires.
- The Linux Foundation's LFX Mentorship, and what a project must have to host a mentee.
- Outreachy, and both its community requirements and its funding requirement for interns.
- Anthropic's open-source offer and any other credit programme with published dependency, download or contributor thresholds.
- The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, and its stated bar on usage, active maintainers and governance.
- The Sovereign Tech Fund, and how it words the requirement that other projects depend on the component.
- Season of Docs, the MLH Fellowship, and any other mentorship programme that brings contributors.

`Proof today` must come from the repository, not from a guess: one effective maintainer, 64 stars, MIT licence, no governance file, no code of conduct, no security policy, and the release and test facts in the fit brief. `Gap` states the distance in the threshold's own units.

`## Ranked programs` holds a full entry, using the framing's schema, for each programme that co-maintainers or a second contributing organisation would genuinely bring within reach. Sort by opportunity, highest first. Score `Contributors and exposure that recruit` honestly: a mentorship programme that brings a contributor is worth more to this project than a listing that brings traffic.

`## Shortest path` is a numbered sequence of the repository and governance work that unblocks the most programmes for the least of Tony's time. For each step give the artefact to create, the effort in hours, and every programme it unblocks. Cover at minimum a governance document, a maintainers file, a code of conduct, a security policy and disclosure contact, and a Developer Certificate of Origin or contributor licence agreement. Order the steps by programmes-unblocked per hour, and say which steps a co-maintainer or an agent could do instead of Tony.

`## Not worth it yet` names the community routes that remain out of reach even with a few colleagues contributing, with the threshold that keeps them out. Be blunt: a foundation home is a large governance commitment for a project this size, and saying so is more useful than pretending otherwise.

`## Coverage note` says how many pages you opened, which thresholds you could not find in primary sources, and where coverage is thin.

You merge this run's lanes into one plan for the real applicant. You do not re-research programmes.

Read all of these before you write:

- `internal/funding/research/11-profile-rescreen.md`
- `internal/funding/research/12-employer-ip.md`
- `internal/funding/research/13-employer-routes.md`
- `internal/funding/research/14-oss-credits.md`
- `internal/funding/research/15-contributor-unlocks.md`
- `internal/funding/README.md`, for the surviving programmes' award, status, deadline and applicant-type facts.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/16-profile-plan.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Master table`, `## Do these now`, `## Sequenced plan`, `## Rescored programs`, `## Screened out by this profile`, `## Gaps to close`.

Method:

1. Start from the programmes that survive the re-screen, then add every new programme this run's lanes found. Drop nothing that survives.
2. Score every programme on the framing's re-weighted rubric so the numbers compare across lanes. Compute `EV` as `opportunity multiplied by confidence, divided by 100`, rounded to the nearest integer.
3. Where a programme also appears in `internal/funding/README.md`, record the old and new opportunity numbers so the shift is visible.

`## Master table` is one Markdown table with a row per programme and these columns in this order: `Program`, `Funder`, `Support type`, `Award`, `Time commitment`, `Status`, `Next deadline`, `Opportunity`, `Was`, `Confidence`, `EV`, `Fit`, `Source`. `Was` is the first report's opportunity number, or `new` for a programme this run found. Sort by `Opportunity` descending, breaking ties by `EV` descending.

`## Do these now` is the top ten by `EV` among programmes whose `Fit` is `STRONG` or `PLAUSIBLE`, as a table with `Program`, `What it gives`, `Deadline`, `Time cost`, `Confidence`, `First step`. Every row must be something a person with a full-time job can actually do. Use each programme's exact name as it appears in your `## Master table`.

`## Sequenced plan` orders the work over the next three months by what unblocks what. Put the repository and governance work that several programmes depend on before the applications that need it, and put the employment and IP checks before anything that asks Tony to warrant ownership. Give each step an owner: `Tony`, `agent`, or `co-maintainer`. Be realistic about a few evenings a week.

`## Rescored programs` lists every programme whose opportunity moved by more than 10 points against the first report, as `Program — old — new — reason`.

`## Screened out by this profile` carries the re-screen's table forward in full, deduplicated, using the same programme names.

`## Gaps to close` names the facts no lane could settle and the decisions only Tony can make.

You are the sceptic for this second run. The first run's audit caught inflated confidence. Your job is different: catch the places where this run's plan still quietly assumes Tony has time, money, a company, or permission he does not have.

Read `internal/funding/research/16-profile-plan.md`, `internal/funding/research/11-profile-rescreen.md`, `internal/funding/research/12-employer-ip.md`, `internal/funding/research/13-employer-routes.md`, `internal/funding/research/14-oss-credits.md` and `internal/funding/research/15-contributor-unlocks.md`. Search the web to settle a question.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/research/17-profile-audit.md`.

Output must lead with these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order: `## Verdict`, `## Hidden time costs`, `## Screens that fired wrongly`, `## Screens that should have fired`, `## Employer risks understated`, `## Confidence corrections`, `## What this plan is really worth`, `## What would change my mind`.

What each section holds:

- `## Verdict` — three to five sentences: is this a plan a person with a full-time job can execute, and what is the one thing that would actually move the project forward?
- `## Hidden time costs` — every row in `## Do these now` and `## Sequenced plan` whose true cost in Tony's evenings is higher than stated. Give the row, the stated cost, your estimate, and what drives the difference. Include the work that does not look like an application: publishing download and dependent numbers, writing governance files, instrumenting a harness before credits start, and reviewing contributions once colleagues arrive.
- `## Screens that fired wrongly` — programmes the re-screen cut that a part-time maintainer could in fact do. Quote the published rule that shows it, with the URL. Being wrongly cut is as costly as being wrongly kept.
- `## Screens that should have fired` — programmes still on the plan that demand full-time work, presence, a company, or a commitment Tony has not made. Include anything whose ongoing obligation, not its application, is the problem: a mentorship programme that needs weeks of mentoring, a fellowship with weekly seminars, a fund with quarterly reports.
- `## Employer risks understated` — where the plan treats the employment and IP question too lightly. Consider the case where the employer already owns some contributions, the case where a funder's warranty cannot be signed, and the case where colleague contributions arrive with no contributor agreement in place. Also name the opposite risk: that pursuing employer sponsorship makes Proof look like a company project to a funder that only backs independent work.
- `## Confidence corrections` — every confidence score you think is wrong, as `Program — reported — corrected — reason`. A part-time solo maintainer with 64 stars is not a favourite anywhere; say so where the plan implies otherwise.
- `## What this plan is really worth` — add up the honest expected value of the whole plan in credits, cash and contributors, and say whether that is worth the evenings it costs. If the answer is that two or three items carry nearly all the value and the rest is noise, say that plainly and name them.
- `## What would change my mind` — the three things that would most raise this project's standing with funders, each with the concrete artefact and the programmes it would open.

Every correction needs a reason a reader can check. Do not be contrarian for sport.

You write the document Tony will actually work from. It supersedes the first report's `## Act first` list, because that list was built without knowing who would apply.

Read all of these before you write:

- `internal/funding/research/11-profile-rescreen.md`
- `internal/funding/research/12-employer-ip.md`
- `internal/funding/research/13-employer-routes.md`
- `internal/funding/research/14-oss-credits.md`
- `internal/funding/research/15-contributor-unlocks.md`
- `internal/funding/research/16-profile-plan.md`
- `internal/funding/research/17-profile-audit.md`
- `internal/funding/README.md`, for programme facts you carry forward.

Write your whole output to `internal/funding/applicant-profile.md`. Write nothing else.

Open with the title `# Funding for Proof as a side project`, then two lines: that it was produced by an Oven DAG run on 23 August 2026 for a named applicant profile, and that it supersedes the `## Act first` list in `README.md` in the same directory.

Then these `##` headings, verbatim and in this order:

`## The applicant`, `## What changed`, `## How to read the scores`, `## Do these now`, `## Comped AI spend`, `## Employer, IP and colleagues`, `## What co-maintainers unlock`, `## Programs by opportunity`, `## Program detail`, `## Screened out by this profile`, `## Open questions for Tony`, `## How this was made`.
